Custom model managers allow you to modify the initial `QuerySet` returned by the manager directly at the model level `[2]`. 

By overriding the manager's `get_queryset()` method, you build a base `QuerySet` that automatically filters database rows to include only posts with a `PUBLISHED` status `[1]`, `[2]`. This enables a clean query notation like `Post.published.all()` `[2]`. 

Because `get_queryset()` returns a standard `QuerySet`, you can chain further query operations directly onto your custom manager `[1]`. For instance, you can run `Post.published.filter(title__startswith='Who')` to search strictly within published posts without re-applying the status filter every time `[1]`. 

However, your textbook does not cover the specific design rationale or trade-offs between using a custom model manager versus filtering directly inside a view. It only explains how managers modify initial `QuerySets` and provide custom notation `[2]`.
